title: Weak-coupling theory of half-metals and other fractional metallic phases in biased doped Bernal bilayer graphene
authors: D. V. Zhitov, A. V. Rozhkov, A. O. Sboychakov, A. L. Rakhmanov
abstract: The paper presents a theoretical study of many-body electronic phases in doped and electrically biased Bernal-stacked (AB) bilayer graphene. We develop a variational mean-field theory with no fitted parameters. For the electron-electron interaction, we employ a parameter-free random-phase approximation to model the short-range screened Coulomb repulsion. The remaining long-range Coulomb potential energy is dictated by the geometry of the sample, behaving as a parallel-plate capacitor. We formulate the theory directly in terms of the experimentally controlled displacement field $\frak D$ rather than the interaction-renormalized interlayer potential difference. It makes our theory better suited for direct comparison with experiment. The resulting phase diagram is quite rich. It hosts several fractional-metal states connected by first- and second-order transitions. At higher bias and doping, three distinct fractional metallic states emerge. We classify these phases by the number of doped sectors and the symmetry of the order parameters. Our results - obtained without any parameter fitting - reproduce key qualitative and quantitative features of recent experiments. This includes the energy scale associated with the loss of fractional metallic order. At lower bias and doping, the model stabilizes a broad spectrum of fractional-metal phases with more exotic symmetry-breaking patterns. This suggests that further experimental exploration of the latter regime is warranted.
summary: This work develops a weak-coupling mean-field theory to map out the complex phase diagram of doped and biased Bernal bilayer graphene. By treating the system's interactions and external fields rigorously, the authors predict the existence of multiple fractional metallic states. The results provide quantitative agreement with recent experiments, advancing the understanding of correlated electronic behavior in 2D materials.
main_problem: The paper theoretically investigates the many-body electronic phases, particularly fractional metallic states, that emerge in doped and electrically biased Bernal-stacked (AB) bilayer graphene.
main_result: The study predicts a rich phase diagram hosting several fractional-metal states, reproducing key experimental features, including the energy scale for the loss of fractional metallic order.
method: A variational mean-field theory is employed, utilizing a parameter-free Random-Phase Approximation for the short-range electron-electron interaction.
model_or_system: The physical system is AB bilayer graphene subjected to doping and an external bias field. The model incorporates kinetic energy, a screened short-range Coulomb repulsion, and a long-range capacitive potential dictated by the displacement field D.
key_observables: Single-particle gap, nature of electronic phases (e.g., quarter-metal, half-metal, fractional metal), and the free energy.
important_parameters: Doping level, applied bias voltage, and the experimentally controlled displacement field D.
main_assumptions: The theory uses a variational mean-field approach, and the long-range interaction is treated as a parallel-plate capacitor potential. The analysis also assumes the order parameter is Hermitian in some derivations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase diagram in the (doping, bias) plane, showing transitions between various metallic states, and show the variation of gap parameters with doping at fixed voltage.
paper_structure: The paper develops the Hamiltonian, derives self-consistency equations for the order parameters using mean-field theory, calculates the free energy, and maps out the resulting phase diagram in terms of doping and bias.
why_interesting: The study of correlated phases in graphene systems, especially those exhibiting fractional metallic states, touches upon strongly correlated electron physics, which shares theoretical tools with many-body physics relevant to AMO systems.
